lesson.title: Following the Leader: The Non-Inverting Input
lesson.summary: The non-inverting input, marked with a plus sign on the op-amp symbol, is the terminal where a rising voltage drives the op-amp's output up in the same direction, the mirror image of how the inverting input behaves.
lesson.body:
The second input lead on the op-amp symbol's triangle carries a plus sign, the non-inverting input. It obeys the same underlying rule as the inverting input, Vout = Aol * (V+ - V-), just from the other side of the subtraction.

Hold V- fixed this time and let V+ rise instead. The difference (V+ - V-) grows more positive, and since it is multiplied by the large positive open-loop gain Aol, the output swings positive right along with it. Raise the voltage at the non-inverting input and the output follows it upward, in the same direction, which is exactly what the name promises: this input does not flip the sign of whatever is applied to it.

A worked example makes the comparison to the inverting input concrete. Many classic op-amps, the venerable 741 among them, have a typical open-loop gain around 200,000. Hold V- at 0 V and raise V+ to just 30 microvolts above it, 0.00003 V. The ideal output is Vout = 200,000 x (0.00003 - 0) = 200,000 x 0.00003 = 6 V. Compare that to the inverting input example from the previous chapter: there, raising V- by 50 microvolts drove the output to -5 V; here, raising V+ by 30 microvolts drives the output to +6 V. Same underlying formula, same enormous gain multiplying a tiny input difference into a large output swing, but opposite sign of response depending on which terminal received the disturbance.

This plus-versus-minus distinction is not just a labeling convention, it is the single most important fact for reading any op-amp schematic. Whichever input carries the signal you want amplified without a sign flip goes to the non-inverting terminal; whichever input you want to amplify with an inverted sign, or use as a feedback point that opposes changes in the output, goes to the inverting terminal. Both terminals draw essentially no current in an ideal op-amp, since the open-loop gain is achieved through a voltage-sensing differential pair rather than by drawing significant input current, which is why op-amps are prized for barely loading whatever circuit is connected to their inputs, a property already put to use back in the active filter chapter.
